newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S. envoy in HK vows to stamp out corruption.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy in HK vows to stamp out corruption.

text.p: U.S. Consul-General Richard Boucher on Monday vowed to root out corruption from his diplomatic mission after the launch of an investigation into the consulate's visa and immigration chief.
Boucher said it was important that the public saw the visa process as fair and impartial at the largest U.S. consulate in the world.
"It's very important to us that our services be clean and be seen as clean," Boucher told reporters at a signing ceremony for a Hong Kong-United States air services agreement.

His comments came after concern in Hong Kong that hundreds of illegal immigrants, many of them from China, may have entered the United States on documents obtained through the consulate in this British colony.

The consulate's head of Immigration and naturalisation Services, James DeBates, has been placed on leave while Hong Kong's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) and U.S. authorities investigate.

With more than 300 staff, the mission plays a key role in Washington's intelligence analysis of events in China and in day-to-day handling of U.S. relations with the "Greater China" area of the mainland, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau.
It also plays a major role in trade ties.

"The fact is that we occasionally do have problems. We've had one case here that's been successfully prosecuted," Boucher said. "We have another situation that's under investigation right now and I can't say how that will turn out."

The earlier case was that of former U.S. immigration official Jerry Stuchiner, who was jailed in Hong Kong for 40 months last August after the ICAC caught him with fake Honduran passports for use in immigrant smuggling.

"It's very important to us that people do understand that we are prepared to go after any allegations of corruption, any allegations of abuse, any allegations of malfeasance, whether they occur within our own service or elsewhere," Boucher said.
"We do intend to maintain the highest standard of integrity within our own service and visa processing."
The U.S. consulate's spokesman, Patrick Corcoran, said on Sunday DeBates, who was on "administrative leave" in the United States, was being investigated along with his Chinese-born wife, Heddy.
Corcoran said the couple were being investigated by the ICAC and the Office of the Inspector-General of the U.S. Justice Department.

The ICAC, without naming the couple, said in a statement at the weekend it and the U.S. authority were jointly probing allegations of corruption and abuse of authority by a Hong Kong-based U.S. immigration official and his wife.
Illegal immigration from Asia, including China, into the United States has long been a headache for Washington.

Hundreds of mainland Chinese are believed to have sneaked into the United States over the past few years with visas obtained through the U.S. immigration office in Hong Kong, local radio quoted unidentified sources as saying.
Applicants, mostly mainland Chinese, were willing to pay for help to obtain U.S. visas, the radio said.
In recent years, the United States has also intercepted several ships loaded with illegal immigrants, many of them Chinese, being smuggled into the country.
Several other consulates have been hit recently by visa bribery allegations in the territory which reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
